exchanges.question: No analyst question; IR asked participants to limit themselves to two questions.

How much of the ~500bp deceleration implied by the 9%-11% September guide is supply constraints versus FX, and what are the broadening supply constraints beyond advanced SoCs? Second: is Apple seeking more memory sourcing flexibility to secure supply and mitigate memory inflation, or to preserve customer value proposition?
exchanges.answer: Parekh: FX is a ~2.5 percentage point sequential headwind to YoY growth and supply constraints increase significantly sequentially, affecting iPhone, Mac and iPad; combining the two gets close to the June growth rate. Cook: June constraints were primarily on Mac, lesser on iPhone and iPad, driven by availability of advanced nodes for SoCs and high demand; very significant constraints currently with limited flexibility to remedy. Memory: paid significantly more in June than March, partially offset by carry-in inventory; September memory costs even higher, partly offset by carry-in inventory (decreasing benefit beyond September) and lower non-memory component costs; beyond September market memory pricing continues to increase and could drive an increasing impact. DRAM market has three suppliers; more suppliers could help supply, unclear on pricing; evaluating all options.

exchanges.question: Expected adoption of the Apple Upgrade leasing program across the install base and whether it shortens replacement cycles for iPhone, Mac and iPad. Second: learnings from the iOS 27 / Siri AI public beta, whether Siri AI drives holiday iPhone demand, and how usage informs compute costs and recovery through iCloud+.
exchanges.answer: Apple Upgrade makes it easier to get latest products via leasing; Apple residual values generally much higher than competitors; offered in Apple retail stores, not widely in all channels, and only in the U.S. (Parekh); uptake to be seen, early feedback quite positive. Siri AI developer and public beta feedback overwhelmingly positive. On compute cost it is early going and Cook does not want to say Apple has a complete plan; there will be upgrade possibilities on iCloud+ for heavy users. No adoption rate or replacement-cycle quantification given.

exchanges.question: How much do supply constraints hit the December quarter, given the Street models 8%-9% growth there? Second: could Apple broaden silicon suppliers (e.g., the Arizona fab) in a reasonable time frame to alleviate constraints?
exchanges.answer: Cook: primary constraint is advanced nodes for SoCs; root cause is a demand forecast issue, with iPhone (+22%, also +22% year-to-date) and Mac (+29%) doing remarkably better than expected; Apple has been pulling supply ahead and will be scrambling on supply this quarter. Parekh: these dynamics plus FX are built into the 9%-11% September guide; no color or guidance beyond the September quarter. On suppliers, Cook said it is not a partner or supplier issue; Apple sources over 100 million components this year out of Arizona as part of the $600 billion U.S. commitment and is pleased with that fab's ramp.

exchanges.question: Will Apple pursue multi-year LTAs with suppliers at pre-agreed prices, and in pricing does it aim to protect product gross profit dollars or gross margin? Follow-up: drivers of services slowing to 12% (slightly below guide) and further implied deceleration below 10% in fiscal Q4; is App Store/AI reprioritizing time a factor?
exchanges.answer: Cook: Apple reluctantly raised prices due to a '100-year flood' in memory pricing with exponential increases; it weighs units, revenue and margin over the long term, not a formula or 90-day clock; LTA question not addressed. Parekh: from 16% in fiscal Q2 to 12% in June, FX was the main driver; also the year-ago F1 theatrical release (favorable to year-ago June and September quarters), mobile gaming headwinds in App Store, App Store business model changes in certain countries, and U.S. court ruling on link-outs (Supreme Court will hear appeal). App Store still set a June quarter record; roughly met expectations but a bit more softness in mobile gaming. FX is ~5 percentage point headwind to services YoY growth from March to September quarter, another ~2.5 point sequential headwind June to September.

exchanges.question: Has there been pull-forward of demand ahead of memory-driven price increases (consumer, enterprise, education), and is it factored into the outlook? Second: does AI at the edge open additional addressable markets for Apple?
exchanges.answer: iPhone has run at 22% growth year to date; pull-forward is not obvious in the data. Apple has now raised prices on iPad and Mac; too early to conclude on price elasticity given channel inventory and consumer response lag; will understand more in the weeks ahead. Enormous AI opportunities; running some percentage of requests on device is strategic and a competitive weapon; no specific new markets named.

exchanges.question: Will Siri AI change Apple's capital intensity given back-end requests to first-party and third-party cloud? Second (to John Ternus): is the competitive landscape changing with OpenAI's potential AI device or a SpaceX AI phone?
exchanges.answer: Cook: hybrid model of third-party cloud and own data centers; Apple has been growing OpEx and spending quite a bit more on AI, with AI costs also in COGS; Siri AI cost impact to be seen, offset by iCloud plan upgrades, balance uncertain. Ternus: reiterated there is much opportunity in the space; Apple focused on its plans; no comment on specific competitors.

exchanges.question: Update on Siri AI rollout in China and Europe and hurdles to launch there. Follow-up: sequential gross margin walk from ~48% ex-tariff refund in June to ~46.5% guide midpoint ex-refund; FX versus commodity costs?
exchanges.answer: Cook: working closely with the European Commission; not yet able to launch Siri AI in the EU on iPhone/iPad, but it is or will be offered on Mac there since Mac is not covered by the same regulations; in China, received approval last week to ship original Apple Intelligence features (e.g., cleanup), more work required for Siri AI. Parekh: GM fell 120bp from 49.3% (March) to 48.1% ex-tariff refund (June), more than 100% explained by memory cost; the 160bp step from 48.1% to the 46.5% midpoint ex-refund is likewise more than explained by memory; partial offsets from carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix; FX minimal.
